title: Reflections on PISA 2022 Results
author: Alex Quigley
summary: Alex Quigley works through the freshly released PISA 2022 results, offering nine numbered reflections designed to move readers past the England-is-failing-or-thriving headline war and into the actual data. He notes the global picture first: the pandemic caused an unprecedented international drop in reading and maths scores, and England's declines track that broader collapse rather than a uniquely domestic failure. He highlights that England's relative ranking in maths actually improved even as raw scores fell, crediting curriculum alignment with PISA's testing style as a plausible cause. Quigley also surfaces the results least likely to make headlines - persistent socio-economic disadvantage gaps, teacher and staff shortages cited by nearly half of English headteachers, and the sobering statistic that one in ten UK teenagers reported missing meals due to poverty. He treats the data on second-generation immigrant pupils outperforming their peers as a useful corrective to reflexively negative immigration narratives in education debates. Throughout, he repeatedly flags the limits of the data itself, especially the roughly one-in-three schools that declined to participate, which likely inflates England's reported scores. The piece closes by pointing readers toward FFT Education Datalab for deeper PISA analysis still to come.
points: Quigley frames the widely reported PISA 2022 maths and reading declines as a global pandemic effect, not evidence of English school failure, since mean OECD scores fell to a similar degree across most participating countries.

Despite falling in absolute terms, England's PISA maths ranking actually climbed relative to other countries, landing 11th in the world - a data point that cuts against the "British schools in crisis" narrative.
He flags a genuinely alarming finding buried beneath the ranking chatter: one in ten UK 15-year-olds reported skipping meals due to poverty, putting the UK on par with Mexico and Moldova.
Quigley cautions that England's PISA sample itself may be inflated by roughly 8-9 points because a third of invited schools and a quarter of pupils opted out of testing.
He credits second-generation immigrant pupils with helping raise England's overall PISA performance, challenging the assumption that immigration is a drag on national test outcomes.
quotes: PISA 2022 scores saw an “unprecedented drop in performance” – Compared to 2018, mean scores fell by 10 points in reading and by almost 15 points in maths, which is equivalent to three-quarters of a year’s worth of learning.

England’s teens saw test scores drop, but ultimately they improved in international comparisons. English pupils scored 492 in maths (down from 504 in 2018), which is significantly above the 472 OECD average.

Too many children in England and the UK don’t know where their next meal is coming from. 1 in 10 UK 15-year-olds (11%) replied in a PISA survey that they had missed meals because of lack of money/poverty.
Immigration is a hot topic, but we need to dig beneath the shouty newspaper headlines, as PISA data reveals that second generation immigrants do better than non-immigrant students
That said, around one in three schools and one in four pupils overall refused to take part in the study. As a result, it is estimated results could be inflated by as much as 8 or 9 points
Wales and Scotland have some issues. Trends in maths see Scotland and Wales make significant drops when compared to England. Reading scores in England and Scotland are far better than Wales
